implementation_notes: C has an unusually precise instrument for this: the linker. Compile with your warning flags at maximum and link — an unreferenced object file is reported or simply never pulled in from an archive, and a `-Wall -Wextra` build names unused statics, unused parameters and unused declarations in every file it compiles. The subtlety is `static`: a file-private symbol that is never referenced is a genuine anchor, but the same symbol `static inline` in a header is instantiated per translation unit and may be reachable. For vendored C libraries, an archive member that is never pulled in is dead weight in the build but not in the tree; deleting it from the vendored copy requires keeping your own patch set.
idiom_name: unused translation unit, unused extern, unused static library archive member
pitfalls: `static inline` in a header hides genuine per-TU copies, so 'unused' at the file level does not mean unused in the binary.
Vendored archives keep dead members on disk forever because the build never notices; removing them needs a patch against the vendor copy.
`#include`d headers that declare APIs nobody calls are anchors the compiler will not report, because the compiler reports nothing about declarations.
